processing: Registered for sencha, and also made as pan-fired kamairicha and as Japanese black tea, each in the usual way for its style.
harvest_season: Spring first flush is usual for green tea lots, as with most Japanese cultivars.
appearance_dry: Sencha shows dark-green needles; kamairicha shows curled olive-green leaf, as is typical of each style.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green as sencha, paler gold as kamairicha, as is typical of each style.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf that opens fully, as is usual for Japanese green tea.
taste_profile: As kamairicha, an elegant aroma with a toasty pan-fired note, deep sweetness and body; as black tea, sellers report a tart edge and spice-like complexity.

brewing.notes: Use about 70°C for sencha and about 80°C for kamairicha. For the black tea, use near-boiling water and a longer steep.

vintage_note: Green tea lots are sold as the current year's spring harvest and are best drunk within a year, as is usual in Japan. Single-cultivar kamairicha, sencha and black tea appear from Kyushu growers, in small batches named by cultivar.
description:
Okuyutaka is a Japanese cultivar registered for sencha, which many drinkers now know better through Kyushu's pan-fired teas. It is grown in Yame in Fukuoka and in Miyazaki and Kumamoto.

The plant moves easily between styles. Sellers from Gokase in Miyazaki describe a refined aroma, toasted pan notes and deep sweetness in kamairicha, while a black tea from Ashikita in Kumamoto is described as tart and spicy.

Brew according to the style in the bag rather than the name of the cultivar. Most of the tasting notes on record come from sellers, so trust your own cup over the label.

A useful comparison is Minekaori, tested with it in Kumamoto: Okuyutaka gave the best yields in young fields thanks to quick spreading, while Minekaori overtook it in mature ones.
history: Okuyutaka was described as a newly registered sencha cultivar in a 1983 research bulletin of Japan's national tea research station at Kanaya in Shizuoka. In 1996 a Kumamoto trial looked at it for pan-fired tea in highland gardens. Little else about its breeding has been easy to confirm.
